newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines devalues currency, IMF offers help.
newsitem.headline: Philippines devalues currency, IMF offers help.

text.p: The Philippines on Friday unnerved currency markets in Asia after it caved in to unbearable pressure and effectively devalued the peso.
It became the second Asian country in two weeks to succumb to currency speculators. Thailand was forced into a de facto devaluation of the baht last week.

The Philippines peso tumbled 11.5 percent after the central bank announced it would allow the currency to move in a wider range to the dollar. Share prices saw their biggest one-day rise in some seven years.
The International Monetary Fund promised financing of over $600 million to support Manila's economic programme.

The peso slumped to 29.45 per dollar after the morning announcement, before the Bankers Association of the Philippines suspended trading for the day. The level was the weakest for the local unit in nearly four years.

The central bank's decision to loosen controls on the peso came after heavy speculative selling of the currency in the past two weeks and repeated denials by Philippine authorities that they were considering a devaluation.
Central bank intervention to fend off speculators rapidly ate up currency reserves and forced up interest rates to levels analysts said would hurt the economy.
However, Philippine shares responded to the peso's losses by soaring nearly seven percent after a four-day slide.

"The whole pattern has been reversed and the public is back into equities. Unexpectedly, the market went boom. This just goes to show you that the market is not dead," said Irving Ackerman, president at I. Ackerman & Co Inc.
President Fidel Ramos issued a statement backing the central bank's action, insisting it was not a devaluation.
He made no reference to his comments earlier in the week that "outsiders" were deliberately trying to undermine the peso.

"This exchange rate action reaffirms the goverment's commitment to do whatever is necessary to sustain our economic growth, control inflation and generate employment through, among others, the protection of our international reserves," he said.
The move immediately won the praise of IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus who said he would recommend the IMF board agree to make extra financial resources available.
A spokesperson said a package would be discussed soon. It would comprise $600 million not yet disbursed under an existing loan and "additional financial resources".
The central bank, which hopes it has now put an end to speculation against its currency, said the lower peso should not damage the economy. It expected interest rates to ease.
It said the economy would not suffer, but admitted it could not afford to defend the peso much longer.
Some bankers estimate the bank has spent up to $2 billion, or about 17 percent of the reserves it had, to defend its currency from the spillover effect of Thailand's financial crisis.
The Philippine move shook the currency markets of its neighbours, helping send the Thai baht to a new low and rattling currency traders in Indonesia and Malaysia.
The IMF said it was not presently discussing a Thai support package although it was in close touch with the authorities in Bangkok.
The Philippine Bankers' Association invoked a rule not used in two years by which it does not recognise the effective devaluation.

Under its rules which govern peso trading among local banks, the rate cannot move more than 1-1/2 percent in either direction of a weighted average, calculated from the closing rate of the previous day.
Any trades outside that will not be officially recognised.

Its average rate for the resumption of trading on Monday will be 26.40 pesos per dollar, and since it was highly likely the peso will move well below that, dealers said trade would have to be suspended again almost as soon as it restarts.
Reaction to the central bank move was mixed. Businesses welcomed the end to punitive interest rates, but some bankers said the central bank had lost all credibility.
"They (the authorities) were very consistent in that they agreed to allow the peso to weaken on a gradual but orderly basis," said Jaime Panganiban, Bank of America head of treasury in Manila.
"Today they destroyed that credibility. This will really be a big setback for this market in the eyes of the world."
